column2: The robot's eyes
The robot's camera runs on its own ESP32-CAM and sends photos over WiFi. This part is short: upload, try it in the browser, then move it onto the robot's head.
Why the camera has its own board

The bare OV2640 camera module you own needs 2.8 V and 1.2 V supplies that the S3 board does not provide. The ESP32-CAM already carries those regulators, the camera and its own WiFi. So the robot's camera becomes the third board, sending photos over WiFi: the brain just requests http://camera-address/capture.
The ESP32-CAM-MB is a downloader board: the ESP32-CAM plugs onto it so it can be uploaded over micro-USB. On the robot, the ESP32-CAM is taken off the MB and powered with 5 V directly.
Address (replace IP with your camera's address)
test page with a photo and buttons
http://IP/capture
http://IP/capture?res=qvga
320x240 photo (for the robot's screen)
http://IP/stream
live video
http://IP/flash?on=1 / on=0
flash LED on / off
http://IP/status
IP, WiFi strength, uptime
While one browser has /stream open, other requests wait. Close the stream tab before the robot asks for a photo.
Set up the camera
Upload the camera code through the MB
Your ESP32-CAM: 5V and GND pins at the top left, flash LED at the bottom right.
ESP32-CAM-MB: micro-USB port, IO0 button (left) and RST (right).
Full code: download robot_mata.ino. No extra libraries needed.
The Serial Monitor prints the sensor type (for your camera: OV3660) and Tersambung. Alamat kamera: http://192.168.x.x.
OK to lock in WIFI_NAMA and WIFI_PASSWORD in robot_mata.ino.
Not yet The ESP32-CAM is still plugged onto the MB board. It must be removed from the MB in Stage 3, because on the robot it is powered from the 5V pin.
Camera failed to start, code 0x105 or 0x20004: the camera ribbon is not seated firmly. Unplug USB, unlock the socket, reinsert the ribbon, and press the lock closed.
Brownout detector was triggered and then it keeps restarting: USB power is too weak. Use another USB port on the laptop or a shorter cable.
WiFi fails: the camera only supports 2.4 GHz WiFi, and its small antenna is weak. Move it close to the router while testing.
Try the camera in the browser
The photo and video show up. robotcam.local may also open on a laptop, but on many Android phones it does not; the IP address always works.
OK to lock in The fixed IP address in the router and the KAMERA_TERBALIK value. Write the address down for Part 5.
Not yet Close the /stream tab in the browser before Part 5, so the camera can serve the brain.
Move to robot power and mount it on the head

Seen from above, the positions match the robot exactly (see the layout drawing in Part 6). The numbers in the drawing are the same as in the table and in the steps. Wire 23 (camera 5 V) goes up from LM2596 #2 on level 1 through the HSV hole.

Why this way? While WiFi is transmitting, the ESP32-CAM can briefly draw a large current. The 1000 µF capacitor supplies that spike so the voltage does not drop and the camera does not restart. To upload code again later, plug it back onto the MB.
The photo opens from the browser even though the ESP32-CAM is powered only from the battery. When the head turns, the camera turns with it.
OK to lock in The camera 5 V wire from LM2596 #2 (female jumper soldered on, heat shrink), the 1000 µF capacitor, and the cable-tie strapping of the ESP32-CAM to the front mount of the head.
Not yet The head is not bolted to the third plate yet (Part 6 Stage 4); leave slack in the wires so the head can turn fully. LM2596 #2 is not mounted on the level-1 plate yet.
